elaine: quick report: production is showing intermittent 401 spikes when our service fires dozens of concurrent calls using AsyncClient + anyio TaskGroup. looks like multiple tasks try to refresh at once and we get a cascade.

elaine: pared-down repro attached below. this is a shared AsyncClient at module scope, token is currently stored in a contextvar and headers are built from that ctxvar.

elaine: repro:
```py
from anyio import create_task_group
from redwood import AsyncClient

client = AsyncClient()

async def hit(i):
    await client.generate("ok")  # sometimes raised 401

async def runner():
    async with create_task_group() as tg:
        for i in range(32):
            tg.start_soon(hit, i)
```

elaine: snippet from request logs showing timing (simplified):
```
[1768130005] worker=10 header=tokX -> sent
[1768130005] worker=13 header=tokX -> 401
[1768130006] refresh started by worker=13 -> tokY
[1768130006] worker=10 sees ctxvar tokY
[1768130007] worker=10 response 401 (server rejected in-flight header tokX)
```

elaine: so even when another task writes the new token to ctxvar, in-flight requests using previously built headers still fail. then several tasks fall into the refresh path and we hammer the auth server.

rui: interesting. two separate issues here: (A) header capture happens before network send, so mid-flight token rotation can lead to server rejects; (B) multiple tasks race into the refresh code because they all observed 401 prior to any refresh completing.

umar: fwiw anyio/trio scheduling seems to make it visible; i couldn't reproduce under plain asyncio in my local smoke runs.

elaine: current code path is basically: build headers from ctxvar -> send -> on 401 async with self._refresh_lock: await do_refresh() -> retry (rebuild headers). the lock is on the instance, not in ctxvar.

rui: a few patterns that avoid the handoff race (ordered by invasiveness):
1) authoritative token on the client instance: keep self._token and always read it under a tiny lock when composing headers. avoid ctxvar for the shared client state.
2) after acquiring the refresh lock, re-check the current token before doing network refresh; if it changed, skip refresh (someone else already updated).
3) use a short-lived "refresh promise" object: first refresher kicks off the refresh and exposes an awaitable; others await that promise instead of performing their own refresh. this avoids duplicate network calls and is robust across schedulers.

omar: example of the promise pattern (pseudocode):
```py
# inside client
if resp.status == 401:
    if self._refresh_promise is None:
        async with self._refresh_lock:
            if self._refresh_promise is None:
                self._refresh_promise = create_future()
                try:
                    new_tok = await self._do_refresh()
                    self._token = new_tok
                    self._refresh_promise.set_result(True)
                finally:
                    self._refresh_promise = None
    else:
        await self._refresh_promise
    return await self._send(rebuild_with(self._token))
```

omar: important: rebuild headers when retrying so the retry uses the authoritative token rather than the stale one.

rui: another edge: if you keep token in contextvar and also have a promise, make sure the promise or lock isn't itself stored in contextvar. we had a bug where per-task copies of the lock caused the mutual exclusion to be ineffective. keep sync primitives on the instance.

umar: test suggestions: add an integration test that runs under anyio with both asyncio and trio backends, spawn N concurrent requests, stub the auth refresh endpoint and assert it was called <=1 times per failure burst. also assert that retries succeed once the single refresh resolves.

elaine: i'll put together a small PR: (A) move token storage to client instance, (B) add promise-based coalesce for refresh, (C) ensure retries rebuild headers. will include the anyio/trio integration test.
